newsitem.title: Central african republic: French battle mutineers in Central African capital.
newsitem.headline: French battle mutineers in Central African capital.

text.p: Army mutineers clashed with loyalist forces and French troops on Thursday in the worsening conflict in the Central African Republic, witnesses said.

French troops helping the government fight the uprising, which has paralysed the capital Bangui since November 16, fired back as mutineers trying to break out of their strongholds rained mortar shells on the city centre.
The witnesses said the fighting claimed the lives of at least two rebels.
Shells landed around the luxury Sofitel hotel and lighter weapons fire ripped through two hotel rooms, a manager said.
No one was hurt but guests fled into darkened streets and the nearby bush as the hotel came under fire at the start of the gunbattles around 3.0 a.m. (0200 GMT).
The hotel is close to the French embassy, one of the key sites protected by French troops based in the former colony under bilateral accords.

"It was around three in the morning when we heard the loud boom of mortar fire. That woke up everyone in the hotel and everyone started running," front office manager Martin Mbekiyanga told BBC radio's French service.
"There was shooting from both sides, but the rebels were firing only rockets. Two rooms have been hit and shells landed in the hotel yard," Mbekiyanga added.
He said French troops had asked to use the hotel's rooftop to get a better view of rebel positions.
A resident said rebel fire came from the Kassai barracks outside Bangui where rebels control the main armoury there.

"Some presidential guard troops were deployed a few metres from the Hotel Sofitel. French troops were positioned a little further down," the resident said. "Rebels aimed mortar fire at the two groups, who fired back at the rebels."
Witnesses said an estimated 400 rebels joined the attack. There were no details of their report of two rebel deaths.

The mutiny is the third mounted this year by troops complaining about pay and conditions. They have now hardened their demands into a drive to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse and to disarm civilian militias and mercenaries from Chad and Sudan they say are hired by the head of state.

French troops helped Patasse quell a more violent revolt in May in which the capital was looted by mutineers. Although France reinforced its garrison at the start of the current uprising, French troops have largely kept a low profile, restrictiong their role to protection.
They have not confronted rebels who have been disarming civilians in some Bangui districts, triggering an exodus of people from Patasse's tribe from such areas.

The mutiny has stoked ethnic tensions between southern Yakomas, who dominate the army, and people from Patasse's northern region. Bangui is divided into a rebel-held south and west and a northern sector in the hands of loyalists and French troops. Shops and businesses have not opened this week.
Authorities on Wednesday cancelled plans for a state funeral for self-styled emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa for fear of fuelling violence, family members said.

Eugene Katouka, a relative and funeral organiser, said Bokassa, who died on November 3 of a heart attack, would be buried in his southern ancestral village of Berengo on December 10 "in a strictly family ceremony".
